I am a landlord by happenstance. I bought my house almost fifty years ago. I recently had to move to a residence more suitable for a 91-year-old, but I could not sell the recently renovated house without paying several hundred thousands of dollars in taxes. When I die the house will pass to my heirs tax free. I managed to find excellent tenants who are taking good care of the property. I rewarded them with below- market rent which has remained unchanged for five years. When the furnace became inoperative recently, I replaced it with a $20,000 heat pump – and no rent increase. 

The arrangement (low cost in exchange for preservation) benefits both of us, but a problem will occur when the property passes to my heirs. They will not have the incentive to continue leasing the house, and the tenant will eventually have to move.

Two days later, he called me. "Could you come back and fill out your application again and just list one lizard? The owners want to charge you $350 PER LIZARD. I don't want you to have to do that."

That was long ago in a galaxy far away. I can imagine how much worse it's become.

comments.body:
“ - But there’s a Tree, of many, one,
A single field which I have looked upon,
Both of them speak of something that is gone…”

(Wordsworth, “Intimations of Immortality”) 

The peasants are dead and gone - mostly - but their perspectives have come down to us in countless ways. The more we care to look, the more we see that Berger’s judgment quoted here, that lacking time the peasant is no artist, is flatly wrong. 

Perhaps what Berger tells us here is that for all his visionary power, he missed what he was looking for where he looked longest, due to the very preconceptions that drew his gaze. Perhaps Berger would have done better to forget the artist - nobodies at their best, scratching and chipping at the surface of a vast labor in their allotted blinks of leisure - and focus the inner eye on art. Berger’s verdict on Millet strikes me as (possibly) projected self-judgment against his own limits of genre, form, and sight. 

I’m a lawyer who’s been lucky to keep glimpses of strange worlds in LA. No doubt I write from my own detachment, but I do know many artists. The best I’ve seen in this house of fame wear the label as lightly as they’re allowed. They moonlight as grocery store clerks, music teachers, aimless drifters. They aren’t peasants, but they’re attuned to their surroundings and they create for the needs of the moment. For their own sake and for their art, I suspect it’s best - beautiful - that they’ll never be seen by the Bergers of the world, or by the NYT.

Berger is attempting to reconcile two opposing Aesthetics, but he’s partially successful: The Marxist aesthetics with its socio-economic emphasis & the Expressionistic aesthetics with its emphasis on the artist’s emotions & feelings.

Berger therefore must justify Mona Lisa’s painting depicting a mysterious smile, as a product of a mercantile class in the proto-capitalist society of Florence. If you happen to find one of the rare large surviving trees that grew naturally (was not planted), you can use the TreeSnap app to report it. Scientists choose trees from this database to propagate and test for resistance to pests and pathogens. Trees with good levels of resistance will be planted together in seed orchards, where they will cross pollinate and produce seeds to grow trees for restoration and reforestation. We are hopeful that we will be able to save these tree species and restore the forest ecosystems that depend on them.

comments.name: Matthew Hughes

Canadian here:

Those who don't know history are doomed to repeat it.

Fifty years ago, Montreal was the most populous city in Canada.  Then the separatist Parti Quebecois was elected to govern Quebec.  Soon after, massive numbers of non-Quebecois Quebeckers fled the province, most of them going to Toronto, which now surpasses Montreal as the most populous city in the country.

Bear in mind, that population shift happened before the separation referenda, both of which failed to take Quebec out of Confederation.  But the people who had left didn't come back.

If Alberta votes to hold a real secession referendum, the exodus will begin.  The effects on the provincial economy will be drastic.  Just consider the impacts on real estate values if whole neighbourhoods empty out.  Businesses will close and relocate to other provinces, taking jobs and taxes with them.

Alberta will become a bargain-hunter's paradise for those who have money, such as US hedge funds and private equity capitalists.  Remaining Albertans will discover that it was the Americans who invented the term "carpetbagger."

The PQ slogan is "Maitres chez nous," masters in our own house.  And they got that without actual separation.  But Albertans will find themselves kowtowing to their new American overlords.

There are people who can talk about themselves--

--endlessly! 

--and we hang on every word.  

Horace (Roman poet) would be one of these.  

Charles Lamb (English essayist) would be another.  

And Nora Ephron would be a third.  

Holding forth till the cows come home.  Never at a loss for a word (and that would include the celebrated mot juste)--

--and best of all! 

--claiming (in all seriousness) to have originated every estimable thing in the busy, noisy world we live in. 

And who cares if she believed it or not?  

I doubt if she did.  I don't--

--but her delightful insouciance as these amazing claims come trotting out--

--gosh!  I'd forgive the woman--

--if she claimed to have invented the wheel.  

"I'm getting no credit for this, none at all!

"--but I had only to look at these unwieldy square things going round and round, bumpety-bump--

"--and I thought:  you know, there's a better way of doing this--." 

Other people do the same thing.  Endlessly scowling, stepping forward, taking credit for this or that. 

And they're dead serious! 

I'm thinking of such a one, now living in the White House.

So we turn away with a sigh.  

"Oh yes!  Him again."   

But from Nora Ephron?  

Never! 

Thanks, Ms. Kemper.

I'm 79 and have stuttered severely all my life. I also developed Parkinson's disease around age 62, which has been progressing as I age. I am now largely confined to a wheelchair.
I question the hypothesis that stuttering is linked to elevated dopamine. Parkinson's symptoms are caused, as i understand it, by a lack of dopamine, and are treated by providing dopamine. I've taken dopamine and dopamine agonists for years and have never noticed the slightest difference in my stuttering.
I did notice a difference when I tried the deep brain stimulation treatment for Parkinson's, involving electrodes in the  brain that produced pulses. The DBS didn't help my Parkinson;s symptoms, and it made my stuttering worse.
I saw an article someplace that described a theory that there was some sort of timing error responsible for stuttering. My intuition suggests that idea is correct. I have trouble reproducing drum rhythms, and my rate of speech often feels uncontrolled.

Cruz's early teens and adolescence coincided with the aftermath of La Movida Madrileña, the explosion of artistic, musical, sexual and social experimentation associated with Madrid after Franco's death, of which Pedro Almodóvar was one of the most prominent figures. In one way or another, she has come to personify the extraordinary artistic richness of the post-Franco era.
A period though so very different from the Madrid where I spent a number of formative years in my late teens during the last years of Franco's life. Madrid then was characterized both by the particularly violent repression of all political discourse and by transgression, an extremely vibrant nightlife, music, flamenco, poetry and sexuality. Another example of how phones can be resourceful at concerts is you can take videos so that you can go back to your camera roll and view what an amazing night you truly experienced-some may also want to send videos to friends or social media as well. On the other hand, using phones at a concert can disconnect people from the awesome and special experience that they spent so much money to see. I think that after paying upwards of 100 dollars for a ticket, having your phone is important for keeping memories, beyond that, it could also be a safety concern not having any way to communicate with anyone else. Imagine you are with your teenage child and they leave to go to the bathroom and get lost. How will they get back to you? Overall, I think no phones at a concert is a great experience, but at the end of the day I think it is more logical to be able to have your phone.

comments.body: I'd imagine phones being banned at concerts could be an amazing experience. I understand the cost of attending a concert and the moments you would want to remember, but the policy of No-Phones-Allowed can allow you to live in the moment and gain an experience without distractions. During concerts, we may focus on capturing the right moment of a favorite song the artist is performing and miss what we're really there for. The music, lights, connecting with the people around us, which is the true concert experience. Living in the moment is such an important take; being more present and enjoying the music can make stronger memories. Others may disagree because the price to come to a concert can take a toll on people, and not being able to share this experience is hard. Especially losing the chance to look back on such special moments. Ultimately, I truly believe that if we could enjoy the moment instead of focusing on capturing everything could really change our experience. Living through our eyes instead of our phones can create an intimate moment that could last forever.

comments.body: Banning phones at concerts could help people enjoy the music and connect with others around them. Beyond that, it could make concerts more enjoyable because people would focus on the artist and the live performance instead of recording videos or taking pictures. Phones can distract people nearby when they hold them up to record, blocking other fans’ views of the stage. Without phones, everyone would have a better chance to see the performance and enjoy the experience together. Although some people like having videos to remember the concert, they could still remember the experience through the memories they make while they are there. Ultimately, banning phones could make concerts more exciting and memorable by encouraging people to pay attention to the music instead of their screens.

comments.name: Mya
comments.body: Honestly, this question had me really thinking about the experience and how concerts are shown these days. Truly, I believe that phones should be banned at concerts. Concerts are an escape and should be experienced as such. You shouldn't have to worry about taking the perfect photo, or filming for your social media. You should be listening to your favorite artist, and realize that your in the same room as them. Find connection with others and make new friends without your cell phone, you don't need it. comments.name: Douglas Van Aartsen

This case is subtle. It is inevitably going to be seen through a racial lens because so many of our disagreements about what constitutes fair educational opportunity are centered on race. But in this instance race is superimposed on a different criteria, economic and social settings. The two do correlate to some degree but should be judged only as racial. 

Compare the situation to sports. As a former coach I often saw Iowa high school teams with considerable physical talent struggle to win championships, while teams with less physical talent won championships because of superior opportunities. Their parents were able to afford "travel leagues" and they had a whole array of volunteer coaches who were able to take the time from work to coach. Plus the expectation of winning which comes from this previous experience is a significant factor in their later success. So if you go only by the "success" of one team you get a view of the "ability" of players which is not based in native ability but in their innate privilege. 

The same is true in educational environments. Achievement by one student in a privileged environment does not mean that their achievement should be a direct one-to-one comparison to a student who does well in a less privileged environment. Often the highest achievers in the less privileged environment will be the highest achievers when put with the others. 

What is being proposed should be evaluated as is a race neutral policy.

I'm so glad we're having this retrospective/reckoning now.

Back then, I was a young cultural writer assigned to the AIDS beat, because my clueless, cowardly editors wouldn't touch it with a 10-foot-pole and because AIDS was a "(gay) arts thing."

I think of all those men who died, all the women who rallied with the gay community to the cause, all the celebrities who made a difference. I think of the young Dr. Fauci, vilified then and now, unfairly so as the science struggled to keep pace with the disease; and the AIDS quilt on the National Mall.

I think of Day Without Art/World AIDS Day, Dec. 1; the shrouded paintings, as if they were Lenten statues; all those galas to raise money; the Time magazine cover announcing Magic Johnson was HIV positive; and a turning point as the drug therapy that made AIDS a chronic disease was discovered.

Most of all, I think of the day when my bosses said I didn't have to write about it anymore. So I wrote one final column about how now that the world's attention had waned, AIDS was even more dangerous, particularly in Africa. I called it "And the Band Moved On," after the great Randy Shilts' AIDS book, "And the Band Played On."

The band may have moved on, but I never will. For the 44 million who have died of AIDS and all those who are HIV-positive, may you never be forgotten. — thegamesmenplay.com

Thanks so much for this insightful article. I was one of those who came to the gay scene of a southern college town in 1978. My friends in New York issued warnings in 1981, and the first AIDS-related death in my town, perhaps in my state, came in 1983 (the struggle of physicians during that time to realize what was happening in itself makes for a story). Every year thereafter I'd lose a friend or two (virtually all of them died), until the epidemic abated toward the very end of the 90s—almost.

Several years ago, I was having a post-theater cocktail at Sardi's when two cast members from The Lion King sat at the bar. They discussed a benefit for HIV victims, and the younger of the pair (gay, the other was straight) said that the crisis was over; he didn't see the benefit's point. My gay best friend, never a lover, died of HIV in 2010 after not being tested for 7 years. I didn't point out my ongoing concerns at the bar; there have been other instances, though PrEP has lowered number significantly in Chicago.

We must also be aware of the shocking withdrawal of HIV treatment across the world through the current administration's lack of support for PEPFAR through the demolition of USAID. Until researchers create a universal vaccine, the pandemic continues. I hope, therefore, that the younger generation's examination of this earlier chapter in its history continues, until that day when science discovers a true cure. Until then, the struggle goes on.
